memory_update.text: Add VRT, ETN, GEV, PWR and FIX as high-priority US-listed candidates for AI data-center power/cooling/grid/site infrastructure research.

This node splits into at least five public-market sub-buckets: critical power/cooling products, electrical distribution equipment, grid/power-generation equipment, utility/grid construction services, and site-level mechanical/electrical contracting.

Follow-up pass should test additional US-listed or US-traded candidates including MOD, NVT, TT, CARR, CAT, CMI, HUBB, DLR, EQIX, CEG, NEE, DUK, SO, VST, CEG-linked nuclear/fuel names, and Schneider/Siemens ADR exposure where listing and liquidity criteria fit.

For FIX and PWR, current evidence supports technology/data-center adjacency but not precise AI data-center revenue mix; elevate or demote after checking earnings-call transcripts, segment disclosures and project/customer details.

VRT remains the highest-purity public candidate for AI data-center power and thermal infrastructure; monitor backlog conversion and liquid-cooling capacity rather than treating backlog as guaranteed revenue.
ETN should be tracked as a grid-to-chip electrical equipment platform after Boyd Thermal; diligence should split core electrical backlog from acquired liquid-cooling exposure.
NVT is a less obvious but relevant component-level data-center power/cooling supplier, especially for liquid cooling, rack power and protection products.
HUBB maps more to grid connection, utility T&D and substation/electrical components than to direct server-room cooling; classify as second-order but potentially bottleneck-relevant.

FIX maps to construction and MEP execution capacity; the key research question is whether technology-sector backlog is concentrated in AI/hyperscale data centers and whether labor/supply-chain constraints support durable pricing.

Future passes should separately test gas turbines, backup generation, nuclear/uranium, regulated utilities, data-center REITs, transformer specialists, EPC/grid-service firms and permitting/water-exposure names.
POWL should be tracked as a high-relevance electrical chokepoint name: switchgear, packaged power systems, and behind-the-meter data-center generation orders create direct node exposure.

WCC adds distributor/logistics exposure to the node; market mapping may be underappreciated because its data-center relevance spans both white-space infrastructure and gray-space electrical supply-chain orchestration.
MOD is a focused thermal-management candidate for high-density AI cooling; follow organic data-center growth, liquid-cooling adoption, capacity, and service revenue.
FIX maps to the deployment-labor and MEP execution bottleneck rather than a component bottleneck; backlog conversion and cyclicality are the primary falsification points.

BE is a high-variance onsite-power candidate: strong direct AI/cloud power evidence via Oracle, but execution, fuel economics, permitting, emissions, and customer concentration require elevated scrutiny.

This pass did not fully cover utilities, turbine OEMs, nuclear operators, copper/wire suppliers, transformer manufacturers, data-center REITs, or grid-software firms; those should be separate Layer 1B passes to avoid overloading the node.
